title: Building security around ML: Dr. Andrew Davis

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's primary focus is securing ML systems against data poisoning, model theft, adversarial examples, prompt injection, supply chain attacks, and software vulnerabilities. The content addresses security operations and defense applications for ML systems, covering both offensive techniques and defensive countermeasures. Threats span data collection (poisoning), model deployment (theft, supply chain), serving (API monitoring, adversarial examples), and operations (CVE patching, dependency scanning). Requires familiarity with ML training, API serving, and neural network concepts but introduces adversarial ML from foundational principles. Recorded conference presentation at the AI Engineer World's Fair 2024. All nine evidence anchors are graded as said_in_transcript, reflecting the speaker's direct claims and cited case studies.

summary: Andrew Davis introduces himself as Chief Data Scientist at HiddenLayer, a company that applies security to ML systems rather than ML to security problems. His background includes eight years training ML models for malware detection, an inherently adversarial environment. HiddenLayer monitors API-level transactions into deployed models to detect adversarial attacks and model theft. The talk covers five threat categories ordered by importance: data poisoning, model theft, adversarial examples, ML model supply chain, and software vulnerabilities. On data poisoning, Davis highlights an ImageNet case study where expired domains from the 2012 URL-based distribution can serve untrusted images. He recommends verifying data provenance via checksums, skeptical treatment of public and user-supplied data, and applying scrutiny to RAG pipelines. On model theft, attackers query APIs to collect input-output pairs and train surrogate models; soft targets leak more information than hard labels. He cites Stanford researchers fine-tuning Llama 7B for $600 of OpenAI API queries. Defenses include observability, logging, and minimizing returned information. On adversarial examples, after a decade of research the best robustness reaches only 50-60%, far below the 90-99% needed for economic viability. Most research focuses on images, but Davis explores VAE latent-space attacks that produce valid on-manifold adversarial examples, and notes tabular data adversarial examples are harder to define. He frames prompt injections as adversarial examples for LLMs, discussing the spotlighting defense that base64-encodes payloads to separate data from instructions, and noting attackers can reverse-engineer readable injection strings via genetic algorithms. Text prompt injection detection is doable via classifiers, but multimodal prompt injection detection is very difficult. On the ML supply chain, Davis warns that HuggingFace has minimal content moderation, and ML file formats like Keras Lambda functions and TensorFlow operations can enable arbitrary code execution when models are loaded. He recommends verifying model provenance, checking download counts, scanning models with external tools, and isolating untrusted models in sandboxed environments. Finally, on software vulnerabilities, Davis notes that ML frameworks like Ollama are brand-new codebases full of bugs, some leading to remote code execution, with many vulnerable servers discoverable on Shodan. He recommends staying vigilant about CVEs, keeping container images patched, and scanning dependencies with tools like Snyk.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Background
sections.summary: Andrew Davis introduces himself as Chief Data Scientist at HiddenLayer. He spent eight years training ML models for malware detection, an inherently adversarial environment. At HiddenLayer, he now applies security to ML, monitoring API-level transactions to detect adversarial attacks and model theft against production models.

sections.title: Talk Topics Overview
sections.summary: Davis outlines the five topics covered, ordered by importance: data poisoning, model theft, adversarial examples, ML supply chain, and software vulnerabilities. He notes adversarial examples are still unsolved and increasingly relevant with multimodal LLMs that accept images.

sections.title: Data Poisoning
sections.summary: Discusses data poisoning with an ImageNet case study: the 2012 dataset was distributed as URL-label CSVs, and many domains have since expired. A Twitter user registers expired domains, so downloads may come from untrusted sources. Defenses include checksum verification, skeptical treatment of public data (e.g., VirusTotal), filtering user-supplied data, and scrutinizing RAG pipeline sources like Wikipedia edit history.

sections.title: Model Theft
sections.summary: Explains model theft via API querying: attackers collect input-output pairs and train surrogate models. Soft targets (logits) enable training with fewer samples. Cites Stanford fine-tuning Llama 7B for $600 of OpenAI queries. Defenses include observability/logging, monitoring for anomalous request volumes, and minimizing information returned to users.

sections.title: Adversarial Examples
sections.summary: Covers adversarial examples in depth. After a decade of research, best robustness is only 50-60%, far below the 90-99% needed economically. Most research focuses narrowly on images. Davis explores VAE latent-space attacks producing on-manifold adversarial examples and notes tabular data adversarial examples are hard to define since discrete features like phone service cannot be meaningfully perturbed. He frames prompt injections as adversarial examples for LLMs, discusses the spotlighting defense (base64-encoding payloads to separate data from instructions), and notes attackers can reverse this via genetic algorithms. Text prompt injection detection is doable via classifiers (AI firewalls), but multimodal injection via adversarial images is very difficult. He recommends assuming worst-case attacker behavior and maintaining observability and logging.

sections.title: ML Supply Chain
sections.summary: Discusses ML supply chain risks. HuggingFace has minimal content moderation—someone uploaded every Windows build from 3.1 to 10 as ISOs. More critically, ML file formats enable arbitrary code execution: Keras Lambda functions contain Python code (can call exec, shutil.run), and TensorFlow can read/write files, enabling dropper-malware behavior. Models should be just parameters but convenience functions introduce code execution. Defenses include verifying model provenance, checking organization authenticity, checking download counts, scanning models with external tools (open source and paid), and isolating untrusted models in sandboxed environments before use.

sections.title: Software Vulnerabilities and Conclusion
sections.summary: Covers ML software vulnerabilities as the final threat category. Davis highlights a recently published CVE for Ollama, noting that ML frameworks are brand-new codebases full of bugs, some leading to remote code execution. Many Ollama servers running vulnerable versions are discoverable on Shodan, making them exploitable with crafted payloads. He notes security issues tend to be addressed after stability, leaving windows of exposure. Defenses mirror standard software vulnerability practices: stay aware and vigilant about CVEs (he wishes a dedicated RSS feed existed for ML framework vulnerabilities), keep container images patched and up to date, and scan dependencies with tools like Snyk. Davis concludes the talk.
